extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics interested in the craft of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on two central novelist's devices: the use and purpose of flat vs round characters, and the selection/management of point of view; also discusses the novel-plot relation (plot, mystery, economy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters (definition and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters (sometimes called types or caricatures) are constructed round a single idea or quality and can be expressed in one sentence (e.g., “I never will desert Mr. Micawber”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: easily recognized on re-entry, need no reintroduction, provide their own atmosphere, memorable and give permanence to a book; convenient for authors because they need not be watched for development. Disadvantages/limits: not great achievements in themselves, best used for comic effect; as serious or tragic figures they tend to bore. Examples: Mrs. Micawber, Caleb Balderstone, some Proust minor figures. Use flat characters as luminous, pre-arranged disks to be pushed into scenes; combine them with round characters to harmonize effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters (definition and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters are complex, possess multiple facets, cannot be summed up in a single phrase, and are capable of development and of surprising the reader in convincing ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round characters are fit for sustained seriousness or tragedy and provide depth and human truth; they 'wax and wane' and are remembered in connection with scenes that modify them. Examples: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky characters, Madame Bovary, Becky Sharp. The novelist should allow round characters to expand and to secrete life unchecked (e.g., characters who effectively 'have their book to themselves').

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing flat and round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel often requires a mixture of flat and round characters; the collisions between the two kinds can produce effects that parallel life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flat people to provide immediate recognizability and atmosphere; use round people for depth. Flat characters save authorial energy (no reintroduction) and give permanence, while round characters supply surprise and emotional range. Great novelists achieve effects by balancing and harmonizing these types (e.g., Dickens and Jane Austen do so in different ways).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for roundness: convincing surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: The operative test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character never surprises, it is flat; if it surprises but does not convince, it is a flat pretending to be round. Convincing surprise requires that unexpected actions or revelations feel consistent with an internally plausible, multifaceted person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view options and their management
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of view include outside description (impartial/partial onlooker), omniscience, first-person/limited (inhabiting one character), and intermediate attitudes; the novelist may shift among these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts of viewpoint are permissible and valuable if the writer can 'bounce' the reader into accepting them — i.e., make the shifts feel natural and convincing. Examples: Dickens (shifts omniscience/partial/first-person) and Tolstoy (intermittent omniscience/dramatic shifts) succeed; Gide (self-conscious shifts) demonstrates dangers. The novelist should place the power to manage shifting viewpoint at the centre of craft rather than reduce it to abstract formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taking the reader into confidence about individual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit confidences from the author about what individual characters 'really' are (authorial asides that reveal motives) are dangerous to the illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such confidences typically lower emotional temperature, invite facetiousness or bar-parlour chattiness, and draw attention away from the characters to the novelist's mind. Generalized confidences about the universe (themes, conditions of life) are less harmful than intimate confidences about individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist's access to secret life and interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: A special privilege of the novel is access to characters' secret life, self-communings, and subconscious states — inner causes that do not have external evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist should exploit interiority (including subconscious motives leading into action), but ensure that shifts into interior description are convincing; the reader cares whether the depiction of secret life rings true, not whether the author can 'explain' it by abstract rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of plot vs story (causality emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is a narrative of events in time-sequence; a plot is a narrative emphasising causality (events linked as cause and effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot asks 'why?' in addition to 'and then?'. Plot development often suspends time-sequence to create mystery; it requires intelligence and memory from the reader and depends on chains of cause and effect rather than mere sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and organic unity in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: In a fine plot every action or word ought to count; the plot should be economical, spare, organic, and free from dead matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist should avoid loose ends and unnecessary material; even when the plot is complicated it should feel organic and purposeful so that, when rearranged in the reader's memory, it forms an aesthetically compact whole (beauty as emergent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery and suspension (essential to plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery — the deliberate suspension of full explanation (a 'pocket in time') — is essential to plot and gives the novel the detective/deductive element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystery engages the reader's intelligence and memory; it differs from mere curiosity, which alone will only sustain a story. The novelist should plant clues and half-explained gestures that gain meaning later, allowing the reader to rearrange events to discover causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader qualities required for plot appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation of a plot requires intelligence and memory; curiosity by itself is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An intelligent reader mentally holds facts isolated and in relation to previous facts, brooding on them until later revelations cohere. Authors can rely on reader memory and intelligence when crafting higher-order plots involving cross-correspondences and delayed revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-conscious method; don't foreground technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels that betray too much interest in their own method (self-consciousness about technique) become merely interesting rather than vital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive authorial exposition of method calls readers out of the fictional experience; better to let craft work invisibly. Sophisticated exposition of jolts or method (discussed in text re: Gide) cools the emotional thermometer.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novelist's skill of 'bouncing' the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to shift viewpoint, tone, or narrative mode while keeping the reader accepting is central: the novelist must 'bounce' the reader into accepting changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful bouncing (e.g., Dickens, Tolstoy) makes logical inconsistencies tolerable; failed bouncing (where the author makes the shifts conspicuous) invites criticism. This capacity is an essential part of craft and is located at the centre of novel-writing technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrivances that spring from character are legitimate plot devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrivances—incidents or devices placed by the author—are acceptable when they arise naturally from character and then react upon characters to transform them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-designed contrivances cause surprise and development (Meredith's examples). A shock that feels organic (e.g., an unexpected horse-whipping that alters many relationships) signals a well-constructed contrivance; the contrivance should not feel arbitrary but should spring from established character dynamics.
